title: From Reproduction to Care: Hormones, Social Circuits, and Parenting
kicker: Reproductive Development, Mating, Pair Bonds, and Caregiving
takeaways: Development has several distinct biological targets.
Chromosomes, gonads, hormone synthesis, local conversion, and receptors contribute through separable steps; no single trait specifies every later characteristic.
Hormone timing changes what a circuit can do.
Organizational and activational effects interact; pulsatile and surge output depend on distinct populations and feedback mechanisms.
Social actions require sensory information and internal state.
Chemosensory, acoustic, and contact cues reach reproductive circuits whose responses depend on hormones, experience, and cell-specific connectivity.
Human identity and attraction need their own measurements.
Sex traits, gender identity, sexual orientation, desire, and behavior describe different dimensions; animal assays or group anatomy do not diagnose an individual.
Bonding and parenting involve distributed systems.
Recognition, reward, approach, competing avoidance, and coordinated action contribute through different pathways rather than one universal social-hormone switch.
Experience can establish caregiving through adult plasticity.
Infant exposure and interaction with experienced caregivers can recruit oxytocin-dependent sensory learning; acquisition and maintenance need not have identical requirements.
